activities.caption: pair each quantity with how you already know it
activities.name: mdQtyMatch

config.prompt: Three numbers tell every journey — match each to how you already meet it:

pairs.right: the speedometer shows its size — direction rides along
the shove you feel when the driver stamps the pedal
two short equations pin the whole motion down

config.why: Position, rate of change of position, rate of change of the rate of change — that is the whole vocabulary of one-dimensional motion.

activities.anchor: a car at 90 km/h is doing 25 m/s
activities.caption: fill the blanks — reading speeds the honest way
activities.name: mdSpeedCloze

config.text: A cyclist covers 300 m in 40 s, averaging %%0%% m/s. To convert km/h to m/s, divide by %%1%% — so 90 km/h is 25 m/s. Instantaneous speed is what the %%2%% needle reads: one instant, not the trip average.
config.hint: Average = total distance ÷ total time; 1 km/h is 1,000 m spread over 3,600 s.

activities.caption: bet first — the curve that steepens
activities.name: mdGraphPredict

config.q: A distance–time graph curves upward, growing steeper and steeper. What is the object doing?
choices: Slowing down — flattening is normal for distance graphs
Speeding up — a steepening gradient means growing speed
Nothing physical — distance can only ever rise in a straight line
config.why: The gradient IS the speed. Steepening means faster; flattening means slowing; a horizontal line means at rest.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the braking stop
activities.name: mdBrakeEstimate

config.prompt: A car doing 20 m/s brakes at −5 m/s². Roughly how far does it travel before stopping?
config.why: v² = u² + 2·a·s with v = 0: s = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 m — about eight car lengths.
config.context: Double the speed and the stopping distance quadruples — the square is the danger.

activities.caption: place the well-drop time on the scale
activities.name: mdWellPlace

config.prompt: A stone drops down a 45 m well (u = 0, a = g). Place its fall time on the scale (s):
config.why: 45 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t² ≈ 9.2 and t ≈ 3.0 s — arriving at about 29 m/s, around 105 km/h.
config.context: After 6 s the same stone would have fallen 176 m — four times as far in double the time.

activities.anchor: a crumpled ball of paper falls faster than a flat sheet
activities.caption: true or false — who falls faster?
activities.name: mdFallJudge

statements.s: Heavier things fall faster near Earth's surface, if air resistance is small.
statements.why: Gravity pulls twice as hard on 2 kg as on 1 kg, but the 2 kg has twice the inertia to move — the effects cancel exactly.

statements.s: Apollo 15's hammer-and-feather drop settled the matter on the airless Moon.
statements.why: 1971: David Scott released both together and they hit the dust at once.

statements.s: Paper flutters because gravity treats it differently.
statements.why: Air resistance interferes — not a law of nature. Crumple the paper and it falls like the stone.

statements.s: Galileo timed balls rolling down gently sloped ramps to slow the motion enough for his clocks.
statements.why: The Pisa tower story is probably legend; the ramps were the real experiment.

config.prompt: From one arrow to two problems — put the decomposition in order:
items: Split the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components
The horizontal component carries on unchanged — nothing pushes it sideways
Gravity steadily changes the vertical component
The two one-dimensional problems run side by side, sharing only a stopwatch
config.why: Direction becomes honest arrows, and the components behave independently — the idea that carries you through projectiles, river-crossings and orbits.
